marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q019.takeaway: At 6% inspired CO₂, hyperventilation continues and lowers alveolar PCO₂ toward normal; above the linear-response range, CO₂ narcosis can supervene.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q019.displayText: At 6% inspired CO₂, the ventilatory response continues: rising alveolar CO₂ stimulates ventilation, which lowers alveolar PCO₂ toward normal. The source describes a roughly linear rise in minute ventilation as inspired CO₂ increases up to about 6%. At higher inspired CO₂ (around 7% or more), alveolar and arterial PCO₂ can rise despite hyperventilation; severe hypercapnia depresses respiratory centres and can cause CO₂ narcosis with headache, confusion and coma.

At higher inspired CO₂ (around 7% or more), alveolar and arterial PCO₂ can rise despite hyperventilation; severe hypercapnia depresses respiratory centres and can cause CO₂ narcosis with headache, confusion and coma.

rationales.b: Apnoea is not the immediate response at 6% CO₂ while chemoreceptor-driven ventilation is active.
rationales.c: Cheyne–Stokes breathing is a periodic pattern, not the expected direct response to inspired CO₂ here.
rationales.d: Kussmaul breathing is a deep compensatory pattern in metabolic acidosis, not this ventilatory challenge.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q020.displayText:
The normal level of ventilation is controlled by the ventilatory response to CO₂.

chemoreceptors.
Option d: The ventilatory response to CO₂ is increased if the alveolar PO₂ is reduced
The ventilatory response is reduced also during sleep.

as alveolar PCO₂ increases respiratory minute volume increases.

rationales.c: Peripheral chemoreceptors contribute alongside central chemoreceptors.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q022.takeaway: Hering–Breuer inflation feedback inhibits further inspiration while the lungs remain inflated; it is most evident at high tidal volumes.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q022.displayText: The Hering–Breuer inflation reflex sends pulmonary stretch-receptor signals through the vagus to inhibit dorsal respiratory-group inspiratory ramp activity. Sustained lung inflation therefore inhibits further inspiration, shortens inspiration and prolongs expiration. It is evident in adults at high tidal volumes (over about 1.5 L). In experimental animals, cutting vagal pathways abolishes the reflex and produces slow, deep breathing.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q023.takeaway: Head’s paradoxical reflex is triggered by lung inflation and prolongs inspiration, opposite to the Hering–Breuer inflation response.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q023.displayText:
Head's paradoxical reflex is stimulated by hyperinflation of lungs. It refers to prolonged
inspiration stimulating further inspiration. Hyperinflation of the lungs causes strong and
long-lasting inspiratory effort (an effect opposite to the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex).
Physiological role:
• Occasional deep breaths which are thought to counteract any tendency to atelectasis in quiet
breathing and possibly in reinforcing the gasps or inspiratory efforts.
• First cry after birth.
• The possible explanation for this could be the inhibition of vagus nerve at cold temperatures
(due to the presence of pulmonary fluid in the unaerated newborn lungs).
• Lack of inhibitory impulses from the pulmonary stretch receptors and vagus has an effect
opposite to Hering-Breuer’s inflation reflex.
emphasis: Head's paradoxical reflex is stimulated by hyperinflation of lungs.
inspiration stimulating further inspiration.
long-lasting inspiratory effort (an effect opposite to the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex).

rationales.a: This reflex augments rather than inhibits inspiration.
rationales.c: The source assigns it a limited role in occasional deep breaths/first cry, not major control of ordinary breathing.
rationales.d: The source describes pulmonary stretch-receptor/vagal effects; the defining contrast is an inspiratory response to lung inflation.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q024.takeaway: J-receptor stimulation produces immediate apnoea, followed by rapid breathing, bradycardia and hypotension in the pulmonary chemoreflex.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q024.displayText: Juxtacapillary (J) receptors are unmyelinated C-fibre endings near pulmonary vessels in alveolar interstitium. Their stimulation immediately produces apnoea, followed by rapid breathing, bradycardia and hypotension (the pulmonary chemoreflex). They do not participate in ordinary quiet breathing and can be stimulated by lung hyperinflation or intravenous/intracardiac chemicals such as capsaicin.
emphasis: Juxtacapillary (J) receptors are unmyelinated C-fibre endings near pulmonary vessels in alveolar interstitium.
Their stimulation immediately produces apnoea, followed by rapid breathing, bradycardia and hypotension (the pulmonary chemoreflex).
They do not participate in ordinary quiet breathing and can be stimulated by lung hyperinflation or intravenous/intracardiac chemicals such as capsaicin.

rationales.a: The immediate response is not tachycardia; bradycardia follows the initial apnoea.
rationales.b: The described subsequent blood-pressure response is hypotension, not hypertension.
rationales.c: Rapid breathing follows the initial apnoea, so tachypnoea is not the immediate response.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q025.takeaway: Moderate exercise raises ventilation mainly through neural feed-forward/proprioceptive drive; arterial PO₂, PCO₂ and pH do not shift enough to explain it.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q025.displayText: Moderate exercise increases ventilation mainly through central feed-forward and proprioceptive drive, not through low arterial PO₂, low mixed-venous PO₂ or arterial acidosis. Arterial PO₂ and PCO₂ and blood pH remain near normal in moderate exercise. Mixed-venous PO₂ falls, but the source notes no known chemoreceptor response to that change. Buffer concentrations are large relative to added H⁺, keeping pH stable; when lactic acid rises, increased ventilation lowers PCO₂ and helps compensate.

Mixed-venous PO₂ falls, but the source notes no known chemoreceptor response to that change.

rationales.a: Arterial PO₂ does not fall during moderate exercise in the source account.
rationales.b: Mixed-venous PO₂ falls, but the source notes no known chemoreceptor response to that isolated change.
rationales.c: Blood buffering and ventilatory compensation keep arterial pH approximately stable during moderate exercise.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q026.takeaway: During vigorous exercise, lactic-acid buffering adds CO₂ and carotid-body chemoreceptors mediate the extra hyperventilatory response.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q026.displayText:
The exercise-induced hyperventilation during vigorous exercise is produced due to the receptors
present in carotid bodies.
When exercise becomes more vigorous, buffering of the increased amounts of lactic acid that are
produced liberates more CO₂, and this further increases ventilation. The additional increase in
ventilation produced by the acidosis depends on the carotid bodies and does not occur if they are
removed.
Note: The abrupt increase at the start of exercise is presumably due to psychic tical and
afferent impulses from proprioceptors in muscles, tendons, » and joints.

produced liberates more CO₂, and this further increases ventilation.
afferent impulses from proprioceptors in muscles, tendons, » and joints.

rationales.b: Lung parenchymal receptors do not mediate the source-described blood-acidosis response.
rationales.d: Tracheal/large-bronchial receptors are not the chemoreceptors required for this ventilatory effect.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q027.takeaway: The abrupt rise in breathing at exercise onset is linked to proprioceptor input from joints, muscles and tendons.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q027.displayText: At exercise onset, joint, muscle and tendon proprioceptors and psychic input produce an abrupt rise in ventilation. In moderate exercise, mean arterial PO₂ and PCO₂ and blood pH remain nearly unchanged, while venous PCO₂ rises as exercising muscle returns excess CO₂. Increased cardiac output perfuses more pulmonary capillaries, makes V/Q distribution more even and reduces physiologic dead space. The later, gradual ventilatory rise tracks oxygen consumption and also reflects body temperature, plasma K⁺ and increased sensitivity/fluctuation of CO₂ drive.

In moderate exercise, mean arterial PO₂ and PCO₂ and blood pH remain nearly unchanged, while venous PCO₂ rises as exercising muscle returns excess CO₂.
Increased cardiac output perfuses more pulmonary capillaries, makes V/Q distribution more even and reduces physiologic dead space.

rationales.a: J receptors are pulmonary interstitial receptors, not the exercise-onset locomotor feedback source.
rationales.b: Mean arterial PO₂ remains essentially unchanged in moderate exercise.
rationales.c: Mean arterial PCO₂ also remains essentially unchanged at exercise onset.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q029.takeaway: Hypoxia closes oxygen-sensitive K⁺ channels in glomus cells, depolarizing them and opening Ca²⁺ channels to excite afferents.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q029.displayText: Peripheral oxygen sensing occurs in type I glomus cells of carotid and aortic bodies. Hypoxia reduces conductance of oxygen-sensitive K⁺ channels and decreases K⁺ efflux, depolarizing the cell. Depolarization opens Ca²⁺ channels; Ca²⁺ influx triggers action potentials/transmitter release and excites afferent nerve endings.

rationales.b: Ca²⁺ entry follows depolarization and triggers transmitter release, but K⁺-channel conductance is the oxygen-sensing step.
rationales.c: The source identifies oxygen-sensitive K⁺ channels, not sodium channels, as the initiating sensor.
rationales.d: Chloride is not the glomus-cell channel involved in the source mechanism.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q030.takeaway: Ventral respiratory-group neurons are recruited for forceful expiration, especially during heavy exercise; dorsal group supports ordinary inspiratory rhythm.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q030.displayText:
Ventral groups of neurons fire, when forceful expiration is needed like during heavy exercise.
Dorsal group of neurons control the normal inspiration and expiration.
Pneumotaxic center limits the duration of inspiration.
emphasis: Ventral groups of neurons fire, when forceful expiration is needed like during heavy exercise.
Dorsal group of neurons control the normal inspiration and expiration.
Pneumotaxic center limits the duration of inspiration.

rationales.a: Dorsal respiratory group mainly supplies inspiratory ramp signals in basic quiet breathing.
rationales.c: Pneumotaxic centre limits inspiration and does not provide expiratory motor output.
rationales.d: Chemoreceptors detect chemical stimuli; they are not the respiratory motor neurons that fire to drive expiration.
